{{Short description|Limit groups over free groups}}
{{Distinguish|Direct limit of groups|Curie group}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[group theory]] and [[Mathematical logic|logics]], '''limit groups''' are the [[finitely generated group]]s that admit a [[Presentation of a group|presentation]] which is a limit of [[free group]] presentations in the discrete [[Chabauty topology]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Champetier |first1=Christophe |last2=Guirardel |first2=Vincent |date=2005-12-01 |title=Limit groups as limits of free groups |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02773526 |journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]] |language=en |volume=146 |issue=1 |pages=1–75 |doi=10.1007/BF02773526 |issn=1565-8511|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Formerly known as '''fully residually free groups''', they arise naturally in the study of equations in free groups and have gained significance through the work of [[Zlil Sela|Sela]] on [[Free group#Tarski's problems|Tarski's problem]]. They now form a well-studied class of examples in [[geometric group theory]] and have led to generalizations such as limit groups over [[Hyperbolic group|hyperbolic]] and certain [[relatively hyperbolic group]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sela |first=Z. |date=2009 |title=Diophantine geometry over groups VII: The elementary theory of a hyperbolic group |url=https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/plms/pdn052 |journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=99 |issue=1 |pages=217–273 |doi=10.1112/plms/pdn052 |issn=1460-244X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Groves |first=Daniel |date=2009-07-26 |title=Limit groups for relatively hyperbolic groups. I. The basic tools |url=https://msp.org/agt/2009/9-3/p08.xhtml |journal=Algebraic & Geometric Topology |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=1423–1466 |doi=10.2140/agt.2009.9.1423 |issn=1472-2739|arxiv=math/0412492 }}</ref>

Basic examples include free groups themselves, [[Surface group|hyperbolic orientable surface groups]], and [[free product]]s of [[free abelian group]]s. A concrete classification is provided by the hierarchy of constructible limit groups.

== Definitions and characterizations ==

=== The space of marked groups and the Chabauty topology ===
{{Main|Chabauty topology}}
For <math display="inline">n\ge 1</math>, the ''space of marked groups'' <math display="inline">\mathcal{G}_n</math> is the set of [[normal subgroup]]s of the free group <math display="inline">F_n</math>. Because <math display="inline">F_n</math> is a [[discrete group]], the ''Chabauty topology'' is the [[Topology (structure)|topology]] on <math display="inline">\mathcal{G}_n</math> induced by the [[product topology]], or ''Tychonoff topology'', on the [[power set]] <math display="inline">\{0, 1\}^{F_n}</math> (where <math display="inline">\{0, 1\}</math> is discrete). Thus one can say that two elements <math display="inline">N, N'</math> of <math display="inline">\mathcal{G}_n</math> are "close" if one has <math display="inline">S\cap N = S\cap N'</math> for a "big" finite subset <math display="inline">S\subset F_n</math>. Since a [[group presentation]] with <math display="inline">n</math> generators can be regarded as an [[epimorphism]] from <math display="inline">F_n</math>, which is the same as a quotient of <math display="inline">F_n</math>, the set of all group presentations involving a set of <math display="inline">n</math> letters is naturally in bijection with <math display="inline">\mathcal{G}_n</math> and thus inherits its topology. One may regard elements of <math display="inline">\mathcal{G}_n</math> either as subgroups, presentations or epimorphisms.

For <math display="inline">1\le k\le n</math>, a ''limit group'' ''over'' <math display="inline">F_k</math> is the quotient of <math display="inline">F_n</math> by an element of the [[Closure (topology)|topological closure]] of the set of normal subgroups <math display="inline">N\triangleleft F_n</math> such that <math display="inline">F_n / N</math> is [[Group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to <math display="inline">F_k</math>. As the space <math display="inline">\mathcal{G}_n</math> is [[Compact space|compact]] [[Metrizable space|metrizable]], this is the same as a limit of a sequence of epimorphisms <math display="inline">\phi_i: F_n\longrightarrow F_k</math>. A ''limit group'' is a [[finitely generated group]] for which a presentation arises in this way for some <math display="inline">1\le k\le n</math>.

=== Fully residually free groups ===
A finitely generated group <math display="inline">G</math> is said to be ''fully residually free'' if for all finite subset <math display="inline">B\subset G</math>, there exists a free group <math display="inline">F</math> and a [[Group homomorphism|homomorphism]] <math display="inline">f: G\longrightarrow F</math> whose restriction to <math display="inline">B</math> is injective.

One can see that finitely generated fully residually free groups are limit groups, as follows. If <math display="inline">G</math> is generated by <math display="inline">n</math> elements, then there is an epimorphism <math display="inline">g: F_n\longrightarrow G</math>. Taking an increasing [[Countable set|countable]] [[Exhaustion by compact sets|exhaustion]] of <math display="inline">G</math> by finite subsets <math display="inline">B_i</math>, one has homomorphisms <math display="inline">f_i: G\longrightarrow F_{k_i}</math> whose restriction to <math display="inline">B_i</math> is injective, and since any <math display="inline">n</math>-generated subgroup of a free group is a free group of rank at most <math display="inline">n</math>, one can assume that <math display="inline">f_i</math>s are epimorphisms and <math display="inline">k_i \leq n</math>. A subsequence of <math display="inline">f_i\circ g</math> tends to <math display="inline">g</math> and has constant <math display="inline">k_i=k</math>, hence <math display="inline">G</math> is a limit group over <math display="inline">F_k</math>.

The converse also holds (but is harder to prove), therefore limit groups are characterized as the finitely generated, fully residually free groups.<ref name=":0" />

=== Constructibility ===
Any limit group is obtained by iterating constructions called ''free extension of centralizer'', then passing to a subgroup.<ref name=":0" />

Given a group <math display="inline">G</math> and an element <math display="inline">c\in G</math> with [[Centralizer and normalizer|centralizer]] <math display="inline">Z_c \le G</math>, a free extension of the centralizer <math display="inline">Z_c</math> is a [[Free product with amalgamated subgroup|free amalgamated product]] <math>G \underset{Z_c}{\ast} (Z_c \times \Z^d)</math> for some <math display="inline">d \ge 1</math>. If <math display="inline">G</math> is a limit group and <math display="inline">c\ne 1</math>, one can obtain the free extension of centralizer as a limit of the homomorphisms sending the generators of the <math display="inline">\Z^d</math> to powers of <math display="inline">c</math> tending to infinity in a way that removes the relations other than commutation with <math display="inline">c</math>.

== Properties ==

* Limit groups are [[Finitely-presented group|finitely presented]]
* Any finitely generated subgroup of a limit group is itself a limit group (hence limit groups are coherent)
* Limit groups are [[commutative-transitive]] and satisfy the ''CSA property'': for all <math display="inline">g, g', h</math>, if <math display="inline">hgh^{-1}</math> and <math display="inline">g'</math> commute, then <math display="inline">g</math> and <math display="inline">h</math> commute
* Limit groups are [[Bi-orderable group|bi-orderable]]
* Limit groups are [[CAT(0) group|CAT(0)]] with isolated flats<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alibegović |first1=Emina |last2=Bestvina |first2=Mladen |date=2006 |title=Limit Groups are Cat(0) |url=https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/S0024610706023155 |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=74 |issue=1 |pages=259–272 |doi=10.1112/S0024610706023155 |hdl=2027.42/135178 |issn=1469-7750|arxiv=math/0410198 }}</ref>
* Limit groups act isometrically on [[real tree]]s for which [[Rips machine]] techniques can be used
* Limit groups admit abelian [[JSJ theory (group theory)|JSJ decompositions]]

== Makanin-Razborov diagrams and equations ==
Limit groups over a free group of fixed rank form a finite diagram, the ''Makanin-Razborov diagram'', that can be used to parametrize the solution set of a system of equations in a free group. In particular, free groups are equationally noetherian, meaning that any system of equations is equivalent to a finite system (this was already known from their linearity).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sela |first=Zlil |date=2001-09-01 |title=Diophantine geometry over groups I: Makanin-Razborov diagrams |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10240-001-8188-y |journal=Publications Mathématiques de l'Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques |language=en |volume=93 |issue=1 |pages=31–106 |doi=10.1007/s10240-001-8188-y |issn=1618-1913|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Generalizations ==
Most of the theory for limit groups over free groups has been generalized to limit groups over Gromov-hyperbolic groups,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Weidmann |first1=Richard |last2=Reinfeldt |first2=Cornelius |date=2019 |title=Makanin–Razborov diagrams for hyperbolic groups |url=https://ambp.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/ambp.387/ |journal=Annales mathématiques Blaise Pascal |language=fr |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=119–208 |doi=10.5802/ambp.387 |issn=2118-7436|doi-access=free }}</ref> and much of it still adapts to torsion-free toral relatively hyperbolic groups.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Groves |first=Daniel |date=2005-12-21 |title=Limit groups for relatively hyperbolic groups, II: Makanin-Razborov diagrams |url=https://msp.org/gt/2005/9-4/p15.xhtml |journal=Geometry & Topology |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=2319–2358 |doi=10.2140/gt.2005.9.2319 |issn=1364-0380|arxiv=math/0503045 }}</ref>
